pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Use a fresh experiment directory outside original stores; do not overwrite original PDFs.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

C1.justification: v5 drops the abstract's sample-efficiency, small-sample superiority and human-similarity claims, emphasizing density consistency and joint ID/OOD calibration. The conclusion replaces v4's unconditional claim of avoiding any ID-performance sacrifice with accuracy close to the parent models and acknowledgment of possible losses.

C2.justification: Biological-intelligence and lifelong-learning interpretations are removed. v5 explains how nearest-center selection, pruning and Euclidean distance can enlarge polytopes and reduce classification accuracy, particularly on non-Euclidean manifolds. Section 7 proposes geodesic distance and explicitly acknowledges the missing comparisons with other calibration approaches.

D1.justification: v5 Tables 1–2 disclose kernel-weight exponent schedules, bias values and regularization settings; Appendix D adds hardware, operating-system and software-version information. Conversely, v5 omits v4's explicit code-and-experiments repository link. This changes the documented access information without establishing that the repository itself became unavailable.

E1.justification: The five simulation families remain, with their definitions moved to Appendix B. v5 adds 46 OpenML-CC18 classification datasets spanning different dimensions and class counts, while removing v4's human-confidence task and participant population.

E2.justification: Random forests and ReLU deep networks remain the algorithmic comparators for the proposed models; v5 extends these comparisons to OpenML. Newly cited calibration methods are not evaluated. v4's removed human study compared humans with RF/DN without directly including KDF/KDN in that comparison.

E3.justification: Reported network width increases from 10 to 1,000 nodes in each of four hidden layers. OOD evaluation changes from fixed square-annulus testing with AUROC/FPR@95 to normalized data and distance-dependent sampling. OpenML adds 1,000 samples per hypersphere and a stated 15-bin adaptive calibration metric, although Figures 5 and 8 label it expected calibration error.

E4.justification: v4's human-versus-machine extrapolation analysis, including posterior estimates along an 82-degree line, is removed. v5 replaces fixed-region OOD confidence analyses varying training size with confidence-versus-distance sweeps, extending these robustness analyses to OpenML in Figures 3, 6 and 9.

E5.justification: v4 Figure 2 explicitly reports 45 repetitions. v5 retains median curves and 25th/75th-percentile bands but omits the repetition count. Its benchmark summary separately identifies variability across 46 datasets. These reporting changes do not establish any increase or decrease in experimental runs.

E6.justification: v4's AUROC/FPR@95 table and human posterior results disappear. v5 adds extensive OpenML results showing OOD-calibration benefits, stronger ID-calibration benefits for KGF than KGN, and classification errors often modestly higher than the parent models. Simulation results are also replaced under revised methods and settings, preventing interpretation as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming KDF/KDN to KGF/KGN, v5 replaces mixtures of class-specific kernels with nearest-center kernel selection and weighted class counts. Neural similarity changes from thresholded activation-distance weights to matching activation paths; similarities receive sample-dependent exponents. The density bias changes from a training-likelihood-dependent quantity to b/log(n). These substantially change estimation and inference.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and discussion are extensively rewritten. Methods are reorganized around a common model, desiderata, theory and parameter estimation. Simulation definitions move to Appendix B, proofs expand into Appendix A, and algorithms are consolidated in Appendix C. The title, author information and method terminology also change.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redesigned into separate forest/network comparison blocks with distance axes. The human-study figure and OOD score table are removed; v5 adds a benchmark summary, six dataset-level figure grids and two hyperparameter tables. Posterior visualizations are redrawn, and algorithm boxes move from duplicated main/appendix displays to the appendices.

R1.justification: v5 introduces a dedicated related-work and contributions section, contrasting discriminative and generative OOD approaches and positioning joint calibration against methods including Ren, Wan and Meinke. It adds calibration, uncertainty-forest and geodesic-forest literature while removing v4's kernel-density OOD, lifelong-learning and OOD-learning references. This substantially revises research positioning.

T1.justification: v4's single asymptotic-unbiasedness argument is replaced by a consistency theorem with hypercube-partition and bandwidth assumptions, supported by bias and variance lemmas in Appendix A. v5 adds an OOD-convergence theorem and a claimed uniform posterior-convergence corollary. The formal ID/OOD setting also changes from disjoint distribution supports to a high-density region and its complement.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially strengthens empirical grounding beyond v4's two-dimensional simulations through the 46-dataset benchmark, exposing both calibration benefits and accuracy tradeoffs. Its qualified conclusions and concrete applicability limitations improve claim–evidence alignment, while added implementation details aid assessment. Losing the repetition count and code link weakens reproducibility, and calibration-baseline comparisons remain missing, but broader validation and more candid claims provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe converting random forests and ReLU networks into Gaussian-kernel generative models. All pages, including both versions' appendices, are readable. Corresponding methods and simulations can be matched despite substantial revisions and renaming.

after.justification: v5 reports original simulation results and experiments on 46 OpenML-CC18 datasets in Section 6, with dataset-level results in Figures 4–9.

before.justification: v4 reports original results on five simulation families and a human-confidence study with 126 analyzed participants in Section 5.

C1.justification: The joint ID/OOD calibration and conditional consistency contributions remain. V6 refocuses the abstract from bridging discriminative and generative approaches toward calibration while mostly preserving or improving accuracy, explicitly contrasting this with post-hoc calibrators. The Discussion similarly changes accuracy 'close to' the parent into 'similar to or better than' it.

C2.justification: V5 emphasizes Euclidean-distance limitations and defers geodesic/CNN benchmarking. V6 explains the geodesic distance's finite polytope resolution and interprets vision results as a compromise between ID and OOD calibration. Section 6.3 newly identifies near-OOD performance as unresolved and discusses known outliers or alternative kernels as possible remedies.

D1.justification: V6 newly specifies 1000 training samples for the ordinary simulation OOD tests, documents the Trunk generator and settings, and identifies ResNet-20 for vision experiments. Fixed exponent defaults disappear from the hyperparameter tables in favor of held-out grid search, without a stated search range. Hardware/software details remain, and Algorithm 1 still describes weighted MLE despite the revised covariance equation.

E1.justification: The original five simulations remain, and Trunk adds coverage of increasing dimension. V6 adds CIFAR-10-trained vision evaluation on CIFAR-100, SVHN, and noise, introducing near- and far-OOD scenarios beyond the earlier OpenML experiments. OpenML coverage decreases from 46 to 45 datasets through the stated exclusion of dataset 23517.

E2.justification: V5 compares the proposed methods with their RF and neural-network parents. V6 adds isotonic and sigmoid calibration to the corresponding OpenML comparisons in Figure 2 and Appendix Figures 4-7. The new vision comparison also evaluates ACET alongside the parent and both calibration baselines.

E3.justification: Section 6 replaces adaptive calibration error with maximum calibration error, retaining 15 bins, and changes OCE from an absolute difference after averaging to an average absolute deviation. Benchmark summaries switch from differences to normalized improvements. Added protocols include a 90/10 fitting/calibration split, AUROC/FPR@95 reporting, and a Trunk dimension sweep with 5000 training samples and OOD radius 20.

E4.justification: V6 expands parent-versus-kernel comparisons into explicit Euclidean-versus-geodesic comparisons for both model families. The Trunk dimension sweep tests sensitivity to increasing dimension in Figure 1, while Appendix Figure 3 adds posterior visualizations for the distance variants. These are new analyses, beyond relocating earlier simulation displays.

E5.justification: V6 first specifies 45 simulation repetitions and adds directional Wilcoxon rank-sum tests comparing final-sample improvements across datasets in Figure 2. Median and 25th/75th percentile reporting remain. The PDFs do not establish that the number of repetitions increased.

E6.justification: V6 replaces benchmark curves under revised methods and metrics and adds results for calibration baselines, distance variants, Trunk, and vision tests. New Table 1 reports KDN CIFAR-10 accuracy/MCE of 83.60%/0.02 versus the parent's 83.70%/0.13, but CIFAR-100 AUROC of 0.69 versus 0.78. These are new within-v6 comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v5.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming KGF/KGN to KDF/KDN, v6 introduces kernel-derived geodesic distance for kernel selection. Section 5.1 replaces covariance estimation using weighted neighboring-polytope samples with within-polytope estimation. Weight exponents also change from fixed schedules to k log n with held-out selection of k.

P1.justification: The abstract is substantially rewritten, Generative terminology becomes Density, and author order changes. Parameter estimation is reorganized into separate covariance and sample-ratio subsections. The experimental narrative is extensively reworked into simulation, OpenML, and vision studies, while the Discussion is shortened and limitations are developed in Section 6.3.

P2.justification: V5 Figure 1 becomes the expanded, transposed appendix Figure 3. Simulation plots gain panels and distance variants; the OpenML summary gains baseline curves and statistical annotations; a vision-results table is added. Six OpenML appendix figures become four displays grouping metrics and model families by dataset, with dataset IDs replacing earlier name/sample/feature/class annotations.

R1.justification: V6 adds references supporting isotonic/sigmoid calibration, kernel distances, Trunk, near-OOD discussion, and consistency/approximation arguments. It removes the Nguyen/Sehwag adversarial-evasion discussion and the Nixon and Madhyastha references. Section 2's central positioning against Ren, Wan, and Meinke remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: V6 adds Corollaries 4-5 asserting suitable forest/network partition classes and Corollary 6 establishing the proposed polytope distance as a metric, with proof arguments in Appendix A.3-A.5. Theorem 1 tightens the bandwidth factor from at most 1 to strictly below 1, and Appendix A.1 revises the Dirac-delta unbiasedness argument. Distance and OCE definitions also change.

improvement.justification: V6 addresses v5's explicitly deferred comparison with calibration methods and CNN-based image experiments through the expanded OpenML comparisons and vision Table 1. Distance-variant and dimensionality analyses substantially strengthen empirical support, while the near-OOD discussion exposes an important applicability limit. Reproducibility remains imperfect, particularly the unspecified tuning grid and covariance/pseudocode inconsistency, but these do not outweigh the substantial gains in comparative evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same polytope-based kernel calibration work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A-D support comparison, including matching renamed methods and reorganized figures.

after.justification: Sections 6.1-6.3 report original simulation, OpenML, and ResNet-20 vision experiments, including calibration and OOD detection outcomes.

before.justification: Sections 6.1-6.2 report original experiments on five simulations and 46 OpenML-CC18 datasets, with additional results in the appendices.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes interpretable message passing, comparable Cora performance, and recovery of cellular-automata rules. v2 makes rich feature representation and superior self-supervised prediction central contributions, including explicit fMRI benefits attributed to positional encoding. The cellular-automata recovery contribution disappears from the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds the qualification that attention weights are not completely faithful explanations, new biological interpretations of fMRI and astrocyte attention, and an argument that AMPNet is better suited to richly annotated features than ordinary bag-of-words benchmarks. v1's delay-differential/PDE interpretation and MOBP–Cryab discussion are removed. The future directions concerning sparse attention, feature selection, and edge features largely remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1–A.5 adds concrete preprocessing, splits, graph-construction probabilities, tokenization/masking specifications, GPU memory information, and per-model parameter counts and training hyperparameters in Tables 5–7. This substantially expands v1's sampling descriptions and brief training setup. Conversely, v1's explicit Adam optimizer and four-attention-head disclosures are not retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds UK Biobank fMRI reconstruction, human-heart gene-expression prediction, OGBN-arXiv link prediction, CIFAR-100 image-network reconstruction, and Pubmed/Amazon Computers node classification. Cora and mouse hippocampus remain, but mouse evaluation changes to masked gene-expression prediction. The six-color cellular-automata next-state benchmark is removed.

E2.justification: Cora's MLP/GCN/GAT comparison in v1 Table 2 is replaced by DGI, GRACE, BGRL, GraphMAE, and feature/graph/random-initialization controls in v2 Table 4. New reconstruction comparisons include GraphSAGE and GraphMAE, with GPS Graph Transformer evaluated on fMRI only. One comparator's identity remains ambiguous: Table 4 names DeepWalk, whereas Appendix A.3 describes node2vec.

E3.justification: Cora changes from supervised classification to unsupervised representation learning followed by linear-classifier evaluation in v2 Appendix A.3. New experiments introduce 50% fMRI masking with three baseline imputation strategies, 20% gene/image masking, patch-based reconstruction, and separately constructed CIFAR training/validation/test graphs. v2 also introduces per-task hyperparameter searches and a stated model-capacity matching procedure.

E4.justification: v2 adds a positional-encoding ablation for fMRI, age/PTSD attention analyses, an astrocyte attention and gene-embedding UMAP study, and interpretable word-attention analysis on OGBN-arXiv. These replace or extend v1's gene/Cora heatmap analyses. The controlled cellular-automata test of attention against known transition rules is removed.

E5.justification: v1 provides no run counts or uncertainty for its own AMPNet results; its GAT uncertainty is borrowed from prior work. v2 Tables 1–2 and Appendix A.3 specify five runs, and Tables 1–4 report plus/minus quantities for AMPNet and comparators. The PDFs do not establish an increase from a known earlier run count, and v2 does not define whether the plus/minus quantities are standard deviations or standard errors.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive numerical results, including AMPNet fMRI R2 of 0.578 with positional encoding and OGBN-arXiv AUROC of 89.5 ± 0.13. Cora's 82.3% in v1 becomes 73.0 ± 3.10 in v2 under a different evaluation protocol, so this is not a comparable performance decline. The cellular-automata attention results of 0.97–1.00 and the original gene/Cora heatmap findings are removed.

M1.justification: The cross-node attention mechanism remains, but the reported update changes from direct aggregation in v1 Equation 1 to a learned combination of previous node features and aggregated messages in v2 Equation 6. v2 also changes mouse-gene embeddings from principal components to learned vectors and introduces patch/positional encodings and a masked-image encoder–decoder, extending v1's two-layer classification setup.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Feature embedding now precedes message creation, interpretability receives a dedicated section, and dataset details, training information, and node-classification reporting are organized into Appendix A. Citation style and the author/affiliation presentation also change.

P2.justification: The framework diagram is redrawn as a multipanel overview, and the cellular-automata diagram is replaced by fMRI/genomics/image graph-construction schematics. Interpretability displays are replaced or expanded with age/PTSD heatmaps, astrocyte attention and UMAP, and word-attention panels. v2 also adds algorithm pseudocode, multi-metric benchmark tables, hyperparameter tables, and substantially reformats the page layout.

R1.justification: v1's extensive cellular-automata/PDE positioning is removed. v2 expands related work into post-hoc explanation and interpretable-modeling categories, adding GraphLIME, attention-faithfulness debates, and other explanation methods. GraphMAE, GPS, masked image autoencoders, and additional biological literature establish substantially different empirical and conceptual positioning.

T1.justification: The scaled-dot-product attention formula is retained, but v2 Equation 6 adds a formal definition combining the previous node representation with the neighborhood aggregate through learned weights. This is a limited mathematical extension; neither version supplies theorems or proofs. The removed delay-differential-operator discussion is conceptual rather than a lost proof.

improvement.justification: v1's comparative predictive evidence largely rests on one Cora accuracy table. v2 substantially strengthens that evidence through reconstruction and link-prediction comparisons, a positional-encoding ablation, repeated-run reporting, and detailed experimental specifications. Removing the known-rule cellular-automata test weakens direct interpretability validation, and the broad superiority claim overstates Appendix Table 4, where AMPNet does not lead on Cora or Amazon Computers. Nevertheless, the gains in empirical support and reproducibility constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AMPNet and provide readable text, equations, figures, and tables. The comparison includes v2 Appendix A.1–A.5; v1 ends with references and contains no appendix. The substantial revision does not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction, link-prediction, and node-classification results in Tables 1–4, plus biological and word-attention case studies in Section 5 and Appendix A.4.

before.justification: v1 reports original AMPNet Cora accuracy, cellular-automata transition-attention results, and gene/word attention visualizations in Section 4. The reused GCN/GAT baseline scores are distinguishable from these original results.

C1.justification: The abstract's O(epsilon^-2/3) guarantee now concerns a restricted primal-dual gap, materially redefining the central optimality claim. The introduction explicitly positions this guarantee for unconstrained problems. The claimed rate and the contributions of explicit, inexact, and subsampled Newton methods are otherwise retained.

C2.justification: Remark 4.6 newly qualifies SSN as an alternative without a universally preferred subproblem solver. Section 5.2 interprets the added comparison as preserving final quality while reducing sample use. v1's detailed explanation of gradient fluctuations and stalling behind the sampling heuristic is replaced by a shorter practical justification.

D1.justification: v3 supplies closed-form implementation guidance for the new mirror-prox steps and specifies kappa_m = 0.1 for the added Algorithm 2 comparison. It revises the documented sampling hyperparameters. MATLAB, hardware, SSN/GMRES details, and LIBSVM access information were already supplied in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate cubic-regularized bilinear problems with n = 50, 100, 200 and AUC maximization on a9a, covetype, and w8a. Table 1 retains the same datasets, sample counts, feature counts, and scaling.

E2.justification: The AUC comparison adds Algorithm 2 alongside SEG and SOGDA as comparators to Algorithm 3. Figure 1 retains EG1, OGDA1, EG2, and OGDA2; the additional Monteiro and Svaiter citation and the text's reference to five baselines do not correspond to another plotted method.

E3.justification: Both experiments now specify the restricted gap instead of v1's fixed-saddle gap. In Section 5.2, the sample-size numerator changes from 160 log(100(d+3)) to 5 log(d+3), retaining the gradient-norm denominator. These substantially revise the reported evaluation settings; the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Section 5.2 adds a targeted Algorithm 2 versus Algorithm 3 comparison examining the sample-efficiency benefit of subsampling. v1 compares the subsampled method only with stochastic first-order methods, without this internal comparison.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. The retained sampling failure probability delta = 0.01 is an algorithmic parameter, not repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Figures 1–2 contain revised convergence trajectories. Figure 2 adds Algorithm 2 results and removes the AUC timing results; the accompanying text newly reports similar eventual quality but fewer samples for Algorithm 3. Because the metric and sampling settings change, these are revised results rather than demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 4.3 introduces a two-stage subproblem solver: generalized mirror-prox followed by semismooth Newton (SSN), with new updates in Eq. (4.10). v1 proposes SSN directly. The outer Algorithms 1–3 remain unchanged, and v3 still reports using SSN alone in practice.

P1.justification: The introduction and algorithm motivation are extensively rewritten, with prose editing throughout. Related Work and Notation become numbered subsections. Existing SSN exposition moves from Section 4.1 into a dedicated Section 4.3 after the convergence analysis, and finite-sum optimization becomes Section 4.4.

P2.justification: Figure 2 changes from six panels to three epoch plots and adds a fourth curve. Its legends say Algorithm 4.1/4.2 although the text uses Algorithms 2/3, and its caption still mentions removed timing panels. Figure 1 retains its six-panel structure with revised axes; algorithm boxes are reflowed.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially expands the convex-optimization context, including Carmon et al. and Kovalev and Gasnikov, and develops fuller comparisons with Huang et al. and Lin and Jordan. It updates the prior min-max complexity discussion from logarithmic to double-logarithmic overhead. Lin and Jordan's 2021/2023 entries represent the same work's publication update.

T1.justification: Definition 2.6 replaces the fixed-saddle gap with a restricted max–min gap. Proposition 2.8 and the descent lemmas are generalized to arbitrary comparison points, and Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 receive revised bounds and radius parameters. Section 4.3 adds Proposition 4.4, its mirror-prox convergence proof, and complexity reasoning for the hybrid solver.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important deficiency in the central optimality measure: v1's gap can vanish away from a saddle point—in Eq. (5.1), setting x = x* makes it zero for arbitrary y. v3 introduces a restricted primal-dual gap and extends the convergence analysis accordingly. The added solver analysis further strengthens the paper. These gains outweigh the loss of AUC timing evidence and the inconsistent Figure 2 labels and caption.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, algorithms, and experimental tasks. All 31 pages of v1 and 35 pages of v3 support comparison, including proofs, figures, tables, and references. Neither contains a separately labeled appendix.

after.justification: Section 5 retains original synthetic and AUC experiments, reports revised convergence curves, and adds an Algorithm 2 versus Algorithm 3 comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original numerical experiments on cubic-regularized bilinear problems and AUC maximization using a9a, covetype, and w8a, with convergence results in Figures 1–2.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same central claims about online loss adaptation and improved training and inference. The conclusion modestly extends the explicit empirical claim from outperforming cross-entropy and ML3 to also outperforming the standard mean squared error loss.

C2.justification: Appendix D adds interpretations concerning information beyond learning-rate scaling, representation expressiveness, the relative contributions of activation choice and online optimization, and validation-induced regularization. It also discusses Meta-LR wins and polynomial divergence. However, D.2 overlooks the SVHN result favoring Cubic-TP when describing exceptions to neural-representation superiority.

D1.justification: v2 supplies Meta-LR initialization and adaptation pseudocode, regression learning-rate settings, and regression runtime measurements. Existing AdaLFL implementation details and hardware disclosures remain largely unchanged, and both versions retain a redacted code-link placeholder.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from four image-classification datasets to include regression on Communities and Crime, Diabetes, and California Housing. These introduce continuous-target prediction across additional domains, with results in Table 1 and regression loss visualizations in Appendix E.

E2.justification: v2 adds Meta-LR comparisons in Table 3, online Quadratic-TP and Cubic-TP loss representations in Table 4, and explicit comparisons against both ReLU/SoftPlus and smooth-leaky-ReLU versions of offline ML3 in Table 5. This substantially expands the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce controlled variation of the adaptation target, loss representation, activation architecture, and training-versus-validation samples for meta-gradients. Regression uses mean squared error and an SGD learning rate of 0.001. Existing classification splits and stated classification hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix D.1–D.4 tests whether gains exceed learning-rate adaptation, depend on neural versus polynomial loss representations, arise from activation choice versus online optimization, and reflect validation-based regularization. The original inner-step ablation and classification loss visualizations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten independent executions with different seeds, matched base-model initializations, and mean ± standard deviation. v2 applies the same reporting practice to additional experiments without introducing new statistical tests or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds regression results and extensive comparator and ablation outcomes. For example, Table 3 reports Meta-LR outperforming AdaLFL on CIFAR-10/AllCNN-C, 0.0656 versus 0.0835 error. Retained classification AdaLFL scores are unchanged, but Table 1 changes ML3 on CIFAR-10/VGG-16 from 0.1027 ± 0.0062 to 0.1024 ± 0.0055.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain offline initialization followed by online unrolled differentiation. The proposed loss network still has two 40-unit hidden layers with smooth leaky ReLU activations. New comparator and ablation implementations do not revise the core AdaLFL procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained with localized editing and reorganization. Sections 3.1–3.2 move to Appendix A, runtime analysis moves to Appendix D.5, and learning-rate scheduling moves into Section 5.4. The principal narrative and contribution structure remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and appendix text layout, expands Figure 3 with regression panels, adds Tables 3–6 and Figures 7–10, and expands and relocates the runtime table. R1.justification: v2 adds references concerning PINN loss learning, loss-induced regularization, and combined meta-learning approaches, including Psaros, Gonzalez and Miikkulainen, Park and Oliva, Flennerhag, and Baik. T1.justification: Section 2.2 adds the explicit condition γ > 0 to the previously unqualified statement that the smooth leaky ReLU output is unbounded. The bilevel formulation and appendix activation derivation are retained; the additional Equation 11 merely expands the existing meta-gradient update.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited ability to separate online adaptation from learning-rate and activation effects through the new controlled comparisons in Appendix D. Regression experiments also strengthen evidence for applicability beyond classification. These gains in empirical scrutiny outweigh localized reporting problems, including Figure 7's inconsistent legend and D.2's overlooked SVHN exception; they do not depend on improved retained classification scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdaLFL research. Their complete main texts and appendices support comparison, including readable equations, tables, and figures. Retained plots and relocated sections can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original classification results and adds regression experiments, comparator evaluations, and controlled analyses in Appendix D.

C1.justification: The abstract's central framework, sublinear convergence, linear convergence, and randomized-ADMM claims remain. Contribution 3 newly emphasizes that modifications to naive sketch-and-solve ADMM are required for convergence, adding a specific qualification to the paper's contribution statement.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly discusses gaps between sufficient theoretical conditions and practice: experiments use sigma=0, do not enforce the new damping bound, and use summable rather than geometrically decaying tolerances. It explains correction-free failure through relative smoothness and replaces v1's unconditional NysADMM advantage statement with a sigma-dependent condition. These substantially refine applicability and limitations.

D1.justification: V2 explicitly identifies the PCG tolerance as an absolute residual criterion, states which subproblems are solved exactly, and discloses sigma=0 in experiments with practical regularization recommendations. Julia, hardware, Mosek/JuMP, sketch sizes, and preconditioner-refresh details are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate lasso, elastic net, and l1-logistic regression using 10,000 samples from realsim. The new correction-term experiment reuses the existing lasso and logistic tasks; it changes a method component rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The main regression comparisons retain exact ADMM, NysADMM, GD-ADMM, and sketch-and-solve ADMM. The new Figure 4 additionally evaluates a correction-free sketch-and-solve variant against the corrected method.

E3.justification: The reported NysADMM inner-solve tolerance changes from the geometric mean of the preceding primal and dual residuals to that quantity divided by k^1.5 and capped at 1. Section 8.3 adds a control omitting the correction term. Sample size, sketch sizes, main stopping threshold, and iteration budget remain unchanged; the revised specification alone does not establish rerunning.

E4.justification: Section 8.3 and Figure 4 add a focused ablation of the existing sketch correction term on lasso and logistic regression. The experiment tests whether removing that term prevents convergence, a question not experimentally examined in v1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed lists, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability estimates. Random subsampling and sketching do not introduce a changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark figures contain modest trajectory updates, including elastic-net curves, while the principal rankings remain stable. New Figure 4 reports lasso divergence and logistic oscillation without correction; v1's separate high-accuracy NysADMM Figure 1 is removed. The revised tolerance specification prevents interpreting trajectory differences as controlled performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 expands from Mx=z to Mx+Nz=0, introduces partial approximation through f=f1+f2, and adds a variable quadratic proximal term to the z-subproblem. Algorithm 3 also introduces Hessian regularization sigma I. These change the framework's procedures and supported special cases, rather than merely documenting the original algorithm.

P1.justification: Prose and proof exposition are extensively rewritten. Recovered algorithms are regrouped under related work, assumptions and convergence arguments are reorganized, and experiments are structured around convexity and correction-term necessity rather than primarily by regression type. Appendix headings and numbering are also reorganized.

P2.justification: The document adopts substantially different typesetting and page layout. Table 1 changes from a rotated full-page display to an upright table without the Year and Remarks columns. Benchmark figures are reordered and restyled, the high-accuracy overview is removed, and a new correction-ablation figure is added.

R1.justification: V2 adds connections to PDHG, further inexact ADMM analyses, and variable-metric work including He et al. and Rockafellar. Table 1 adds Hager and Zhang and removes the QPALM comparison rows, although QPALM remains cited in the text. The central positioning around convergence of randomized approximate ADMM remains.

T1.justification: V2 replaces assumed iterate boundedness with Proposition 3 and its Appendix A.2 argument, revises metric and regularity assumptions, and extends the ergodic analysis. The linear-convergence proof replaces gradient-error forcing and the earlier two-variable contraction with a full-iterate Lyapunov and coupling analysis. It introduces whole-space, operator-invertibility, and Theta_min>L_f^2/sigma_f conditions and replaces the earlier optimized rate expression. Supporting appendix proofs are substantially revised.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens the analytical foundation by supplying a boundedness argument that v1 assumed and rebuilding the convergence analysis for a broader framework. C1.justification: The introduction adds claims of tighter sub-Gaussian concentration and an extension to time-varying means, materially broadening the contributions beyond v1's constant-mean constructions. It also qualifies the blanket closed-form claim by explicitly excluding the implicit robust heavy-tail result.

C2.justification: v1 suggests fully empirical heavy-tail bounds as future work; v2 Section 3.1 instead explains why known variance information is necessary and why empirical variance terms may fail to concentrate. v2 also acknowledges dimension dependence of the revised robust construction and explicitly identifies the less favorable dimension/logarithm separation in its stitched bound compared with Manole and Ramdas.

D1.justification: v2 supplies explicit tuning guidance for new constructions, including the Gaussian precision choice for Corollary 2, epoch weights in Appendix A.3, and constant-weight behavior for robust heavy-tail bounds. Neither PDF provides simulation code, and the new mixtures' component parameters and weights are not fully specified.

E1.justification: The simulations retain multivariate mean estimation but revise synthetic distribution coverage: v1's Beta(50,10) example disappears, while v2 introduces mixtures of betas and binomials. Uniform and Beta(10,10) examples remain. The new time-varying-mean theory is not accompanied by an empirical evaluation.

E2.justification: v2 Figure 1 adds an oracle multivariate Bernstein comparator, attributed to Gross (2011) and Kohler and Lucchi (2017), for the bounded-data comparison. The median-of-means comparator remains in the Catoni–Giulini comparison.

E3.justification: v2 adds a fixed-time convergence evaluation with alpha = 0.05 and d = 2, and extends the median-of-means comparison from d = 20 to d = 5, 20, and 100. The latter retains the alpha/(t+t²) union-bound procedure. The new Bernstein comparison introduces oracle variance information as a control.

E4.justification: v2 adds a numerical illustration of convergence toward the existing asymptotic-width result and extends the dimension-sensitivity analysis of the heavy-tail comparison. Variance-adaptation illustrations remain, with revised distributions. Neither version reports an empirical contamination-robustness test.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 1 explicitly reports standard-deviation bands across 100 trials. v1 supplies neither corresponding variability bands nor a repeated-run count. This establishes new uncertainty reporting, without establishing an increase in runs for a retained experiment.

E6.justification: v2 adds convergence results, oracle-versus-empirical Bernstein curves for the revised distributions, and heavy-tail comparison curves at additional dimensions. The qualitative findings of variance adaptation and narrower Catoni–Giulini bounds than union-bounded median-of-means remain. These additions do not establish a same-setting performance improvement between versions.

M1.justification: v2 adds Gaussian-based sub-Gaussian confidence spheres, a Gaussian-mixture construction for time-varying means, and a conditional-symmetry construction for heavy tails. It also revises semi-empirical and robust radius formulas. The thresholded Catoni–Giulini estimator itself remains unchanged, moving from Theorem 3 to Theorem 6.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: Sections 3 and 4 gain thematic subsections, revised material from v1 Appendices B–C enters the main text, the anisotropy discussion moves to Appendix B, and Catoni proof development moves into Appendix D. The introduction, related work, explanations, and conclusion are extensively revised.

P2.justification: The main figures are redesigned into a three-panel Figure 1 combining convergence, Bernstein comparisons, and heavy-tail comparisons. The original density panel is removed, and uncertainty shading, legends, and a logarithmic time axis are introduced. The vMF plot is retained and renumbered. The heavy-tail legend incorrectly retains 'Theorem 3' although that result is now Theorem 6.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially through comparisons with oracle Bernstein bounds, classical sub-Gaussian concentration, and Gaussian-mixture methods, adding works including Gross, Kohler–Lucchi, Jin et al., Rigollet–Hütter, and Robbins. The self-normalized-work discussion is rewritten, and new Appendix C derives the relationship to Wang and Ramdas. Publication updates to existing references are not new works.

T1.justification: v2 adds sub-Gaussian and conditional-symmetry theorems, the time-varying-mean proposition, and a sub-Gaussian stitching derivation in Appendix A.3. It also corrects substantive mathematics: v1 Appendix C's Gaussian second-moment expression d/β² becomes d/β+1 in v2 Appendix D.2, changing the semi-empirical bound. v1 Appendix B's robust bound with a constant 2C term is replaced by a dimension-dependent bound containing t·epsilon·(exp(C)−exp(−C)), with an explicit proof in Appendix D.3.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important mathematical deficiencies in v1 Appendices B–C, correcting Gaussian moment calculations and contamination accounting while supplying fuller proofs. These repairs, useful new inferential constructions, and clearer applicability limits substantially improve the paper's reliability and scope. Some revised guarantees are more conservative, appropriately reflecting their assumptions. Incomplete mixture specifications and the stale figure legend remain limited weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same confidence-sphere research. Their complete text, equations, figures, and Appendices A–F support comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 Figure 1 reports simulations with Beta variables and beta-binomial mixtures, including variability across 100 trials.

before.justification: v1 Figure 1 reports confidence-sphere widths calculated from sampled Beta-distributed random vectors, providing original simulation results.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion shift from emphasizing empirical-Bernstein and Huber-robust extensions to dimension-free sub-Gaussian, log-concave, and heavy-tailed results. Huber-robust contribution claims disappear, and the retained empirical-Bernstein result becomes secondary.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning fixed beta, known covariance bounds, the log-concave constant C, and raw versus centered moment assumptions. It explains the revised dimension dependence and characterizes its empirical-Bernstein bound as suboptimal relative to newer work. Huber-specific interpretations and the explicit fixed-dimension caveat accompanying the earlier empirical-Bernstein asymptotics disappear.

D1.justification: Section 2.1 adds covariance-dependent tuning formulas for beta and lambda, and Appendix C.1 specifies the truncated-Gaussian covariance and radius. Huber-specific tuning guidance in v2 Section 4 and Appendix F.2 is removed. These concern applying the constructions, rather than documented changes to the numerical experiments.

E1.justification: The numerical illustrations retain the Beta(10,10), uniform, beta/binomial-mixture, and zero-mean identity-covariance settings. The new log-concave and anisotropic results extend theoretical coverage without adding evaluated data or scenarios.

E2.justification: The numerical comparisons retain the oracle Bernstein bounds attributed to Gross and Kohler–Lucchi and the median-of-means estimator made time-uniform by a union bound. New discussions of other concentration results do not add numerically evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Reported settings remain unchanged: the Beta illustration uses alpha=0.05 and d=2, while the heavy-tail comparison retains d=5,20,100 and the MoM correction alpha/(t+t²). No protocol revision accompanies the small change in plotted MoM widths.

E4.justification: Both versions retain the same numerical investigations of asymptotic width, variance adaptation, and dimension-dependent confidence widths. No ablation, robustness experiment, or additional supplementary numerical analysis is added or removed.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 1 and v3 Figure 2 both report shaded standard deviations across 100 trials. Neither version adds different run counts, seed information, or statistical testing practices.

E6.justification: The MoM reference widths change slightly between v2 Figure 1's right panel and v3 Figure 1: for d=100 near t=1, the plotted width increases approximately from 33.4 to 34.2. Catoni-Giulini curves and the ranking remain essentially unchanged. The empirical-Bernstein and vMF plots are identical.

M1.justification: v3 adds a truncated-Gaussian construction for log-concave confidence spheres and revises confidence-radius procedures to use covariance information and remove dimension factors. It removes both Huber-robust constructions from v2 Section 4. The underlying weighted-mean and thresholded Catoni-Giulini point estimators remain.

P1.justification: The abstract and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten. Light-tailed results are reorganized, empirical-Bernstein material and its asymptotic appendix are consolidated into Appendix A, ellipsoid discussion moves into Section 2.6, and the two semi-empirical bounds receive separate subsections. The robustness section and associated appendices disappear.

P2.justification: v3 adds the results roadmap in Table 1 and splits v2's three-panel Figure 1 into Figures 1 and 2. The heavy-tail legend expands 'MoM' and replaces the misleading 'Theorem 3' label with 'Sequential CG'. The vMF plot is relocated and renumbered; the basic document layout remains similar.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts toward dimension-free variational concentration, with substantive new discussions of Hsu et al., Zhivotovskiy, Nakakita et al., Giulini, and Duchi–Haque. Appendix A acknowledges Martinez-Taboada–Ramdas's dimension-free empirical-Bernstein result. The robustness literature discussion and comparison appendix concerning Huber-robust Wang–Ramdas bounds are removed.

T1.justification: v3 adds the log-concave theorem and proof, generalizes sub-Gaussian and sub-psi bounds to covariance-based assumptions, and rederives Theorems 4 and 5 without explicit dimension factors. Stitched bounds are revised. Huber-robust results and proofs, the dedicated empirical-Bernstein stitching proposition, and the heavy-tail ellipsoid construction are removed. Nonrobust empirical-Bernstein asymptotics and vMF lemmas are retained.

improvement.justification: Sharper Gaussian integration in Appendix C.2 removes avoidable dimension penalties from the retained heavy-tailed bounds, resolving a substantial theoretical weakness. Covariance-sensitive sub-Gaussian bounds and the log-concave construction further strengthen the central framework, with clearer applicability discussions. Removing both Huber-robust extensions narrows scope, and reporting flaws remain, including missing second-moment squares in Table 1. Nevertheless, the improvements to the retained central theory are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 44 pages of v2 and 41 pages of v3, including appendices, equations, figures, and references, support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original numerical results in Appendix A, Figure 2, including the 100-trial comparison.

before.justification: v2 Figure 1 reports original numerical illustrations of empirical-Bernstein confidence widths, including standard deviations across 100 trials.

C1.justification: The abstract newly claims optimality, and the introduction and conclusion foreground explicit iterated-logarithm guarantees across additional cases. The auxiliary vMF contribution is dropped. V4 also explicitly advertises applicability beyond log-concavity to bounded Orlicz norm, although the underlying norm condition already appeared in v3 Theorem 2.

C2.justification: V4 adds explanations connecting Hsu’s competitiveness to covariance-spectrum terms and tournament MoM’s practical weakness to large constants. It discusses the distinction between knowing variance and knowing a raw second-moment bound, and compares the applicability of Orlicz-based and isotropic sub-exponential bounds. Principal limitations concerning known bounds and heavy-tail assumptions remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix C supplies a code-repository reference, explicit weighting and tuning choices, comparator formulas, and error allocations for union-bound and doubling constructions. V3 offered theoretical tuning advice but no corresponding simulation-details appendix or code-access statement. These are substantial documentation additions; the repository’s availability was not externally checked.

E1.justification: V4 Figure 1 adds numerical evaluation of sub-Gaussian bounds across covariance regimes. The task remains sequential mean estimation, and the bounded beta/binomial simulation coverage is retained. Newly discussed theoretical distribution classes do not constitute additional evaluated datasets.

E2.justification: V4 expands the earlier median-of-means comparison by adding geometric median-of-means (Minsker, 2015) alongside tournament median-of-means, and evaluates doubling variants as well as naive union bounds. Hsu et al. (2012), previously discussed theoretically, becomes an evaluated comparator in Figure 1. The empirical-Bernstein oracle comparators are retained.

E3.justification: The heavy-tail comparison changes from identity-covariance curves for d = 5, 20 and 100 through t = 10,000 to comparisons through t = 100,000, including matched trace and second-moment bounds of 5. These are revised comparison settings. V4 Figure 1 remains ambiguously specified: its caption gives covariance trace 5, whereas Appendix C gives 1 for the left panel.

E4.justification: V4 adds a covariance-ratio sensitivity analysis identifying regimes favorable to Hsu’s doubled bound, together with stitched versus unstitched comparisons. The earlier heavy-tail dimension sweep is removed. Figure 2’s enlarged GMoM panel redisplays a subset of the comparison rather than adding a separate analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard-deviation shading across 100 trials for the retained empirical-Bernstein simulations. No new seed information, replication counts, significance tests or uncertainty-reporting practice is documented for the added numerical bound comparisons.

E6.justification: New sub-Gaussian curves show the stitched bound outperforming the unstitched bound, while Hsu with doubling can be tighter at small covariance ratios. Revised heavy-tail comparisons show GMoM sometimes beating unstitched Catoni–Giulini, while stitched Catoni–Giulini dominates the plotted alternatives. These are added or reworked comparisons, not controlled cross-version performance gains. The empirical-Bernstein plots are identical.

M1.justification: V4 replaces the von Mises–Fisher constructions with uniform distributions for the sub-ψ, time-varying-mean and empirical-Bernstein bounds, changing their computable formulas and tuning parameters. It also introduces a stitched Catoni–Giulini construction in Theorem 3.8. The underlying Catoni–Giulini truncation estimator is retained.

P1.justification: The title and main Introduction–Light tails–Heavy tails–Summary organization remain. V4 makes focused explanatory rewrites, removes the vMF interlude, reorganizes the appendices, adds a simulation-details section and adopts section-based theorem numbering. Much of the existing exposition is retained.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains rows and LIL/fixed-time-optimization columns. V4 adds a two-panel sub-Gaussian figure and replaces the heavy-tail inset with a larger two-panel comparison. The empirical-Bernstein figure moves unchanged, while the vMF illustration disappears. Several new plot legends retain obsolete theorem numbers, creating cross-reference inconsistencies.

R1.justification: V4 adds Minsker (2015) and Lee et al. (2024), removes vMF-related references, and refines its comparisons with Hsu, Manole–Ramdas and Duchi–Haque. The central PAC-Bayesian positioning remains. The Waudby-Smith et al. 2021-to-2024 reference change identifies the same work’s publication update.

T1.justification: V4 revises the sub-Gaussian assumption to permit adapted covariance processes and replaces the vMF-based derivations. Sub-Gaussian and sub-gamma stitching already existed in v3 Appendix B; v4 strengthens those bounds and adds explicit sub-exponential, log-concave and Catoni–Giulini stitching proofs. It also adds Hsu-comparison and covariance-spectrum lemmas, and re-derives the empirical-Bernstein bound and its asymptotic width.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens v3’s coarse stitched guarantees and limited comparative evidence through sharper explicit bounds, additional proofs, and stronger Hsu/GMoM/doubling comparisons that reveal both advantages and unfavorable regimes. Appendix C materially improves reproducibility information. These gains outweigh the Figure 1 covariance-setting contradiction and obsolete plot labels, which still impair reproducibility and clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same title, authors and sequential mean-estimation objective. All 41 pages of v3 and 46 pages of v4, including appendices, support comparison. Relocated material and renumbered results can be matched.

after.justification: Appendix D, Figure 3 retains those original simulations. Figures 1–2 additionally report numerical comparisons of confidence-bound widths.

before.justification: Appendix A, Figure 2 reports original simulations using beta-distributed vectors and beta/binomial mixtures, including standard deviations across 100 trials.

This substantially improves the justification and applicability guidance for the confidence guarantees. The general bound is looser, but that tradeoff is explicit; the existing simulation evidence is preserved.

C1.justification: v1 principally claims improvements to PAWS/RoPAWS and few-label classification. v2 presents PAWS-VMK as a joint SSL/OOD approach competitive with specialized detectors, making OOD detection central to the title, abstract and introduction. This capability was only proposed for future investigation in v1's discussion.

C2.justification: v2 introduces explanations linking the components to compact prototype clusters, improved class separation and OOD detection. Appendix A interprets backbone-versus-projection differences through DINOv2's pretraining exposure, while Appendix B identifies dataset-dependent hyperparameter preferences. v1's speculative distillation, adversarial-robustness and multimodal-LLM discussion is removed. The retained blanket SKMPS superiority wording is less consistent with v2 Table 4's CIFAR-100 ordering.

D1.justification: v2 adds GPU memory capacity and timing information for larger backbones while retaining most implementation details and hyperparameter tables in Appendices C–D. It omits v1's explicit best-validation-epoch/test-reporting rule and Food-101 run-exclusion explanation. The PDFs do not explain how the previously excluded USL Food-101 runs became reportable.

E1.justification: v2 adds OOD detection around CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, using Tiny ImageNet and the opposite CIFAR dataset for near OOD, and Places365, DTD, MNIST and SVHN for far OOD. The seven original classification datasets, binary DeepWeeds task and cross-dataset pretraining coverage are retained.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds +SemiReward and Semi-ViT comparisons and drops v1 Table 2's CIFAR-100 comparison attributed to Shrinking Class Space. The new OOD comparison includes DeepEnsemble, KNN, CIDER, LogitNorm, PixMix and PALM. USL also gains reported Food-101 comparisons, which v1 left unreported.

E3.justification: v2 expands model settings from DINOv2 ViT-S/14 to include ViT-B/14 and ViT-L/14. It introduces near/far OpenOOD evaluation with AUROC and FPR reporting and a Gaussian-kernel control. The original classification label budgets, stated splits, and 50-epoch training/20-epoch pretraining budgets remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds OOD component ablations, backbone-versus-projection OOD comparisons, and embedding/density analyses in Figures 4–6. Head/loss ablations expand to CIFAR-100 and Food-101. The original hyperparameter study becomes Table S6, adding those datasets and a Gaussian-kernel comparison. Transfer-learning and RoPAWS studies are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions retain five-run means and standard deviations, 20-run prototype-diversity plots with minimum/maximum bars, and mainly single-run nondefault hyperparameter tests. No new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is specified. Additional result rows and changed uncertainty values do not establish a changed statistical procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds OOD and larger-backbone results and revises retained classification, transfer, RoPAWS and kNN entries. For example, the modified method's CIFAR-100 result changes from 73.6±1.2 in v1 Table 2 to 75.7±0.9 in v2 Table 3 alongside the loss revision. USL/SKMPS means reverse order: 76.3/76.6 in v1 Table 3 versus 77.5/77.3 in v2 Table 4. Larger-model headline accuracies are not same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The pseudolabel target changes from a sharpened geometric combination of predictions in v1 Equation 21 to a sharpened arithmetic average in v2 Equation 9. v2 also specifies maximum prototype cosine similarity for OOD scoring. These are limited procedural changes; the overall frozen-backbone/projector design, vMF-SNE pretraining and k-means selection procedure remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and discussion are substantially rewritten around OOD detection. PAWS background moves into methodological preliminaries, and several original main-text studies move into reorganized appendices. PAWS-VM/VMK and SKMPS terminology accompanies this broader narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 changes from a two-column to a single-column format and adds a framework diagram, OOD tables and embedding/density figures. Original Figure 2 is split between an expanded main-text ablation figure and supplementary training curves. Several tables move to the supplement, and the hyperparameter tables are spread across multiple pages.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts toward the intersection of SSL and OOD detection, with substantial new coverage including OpenOOD, PALM, SemiReward and several OOD comparison methods. CIDER, already cited prospectively in v1, becomes a central comparator. The earlier emphasis on biological concept learning and knowledge distillation is removed or reduced.

T1.justification: The formal multiview target and loss definition changes between v1 Equations 21–22 and v2 Equation 9. v1's explicit Gaussian/Student-t SNE and distillation derivations are also removed. The central PAWS probability derivation and vMF-SNE construction remain substantially unchanged, with no new theorem or proof development.

improvement.justification: The Gaussian-kernel control, broader sensitivity tests and additional component ablations substantially strengthen support for the design choices. OOD experiments replace v1's speculation with benchmark, component and backbone comparisons, making applicability more assessable. These gains outweigh the unexplained Food-101 reporting change and overly broad SKMPS superiority wording, although those issues limit reproducibility and claim precision.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and emphasis, both PDFs describe the same PAWS-based research framework. Their complete main texts and supplements support matching the methods, equations, experiments, tables and figures.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification experiments and additional OOD detection, component-ablation and embedding analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, pretraining, prototype-selection, transfer-learning and RoPAWS experiments, including supplementary sensitivity analyses.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claims: entropy-rate minimization through a learned surrogate trades reward against predictability and produces more predictable, near-optimal policies in robotic and driving tasks. The average-reward connection emphasized in v4's abstract was already a stated contribution in v2.

C2.justification: v4 explains negative continuous-space values through differential entropy, interprets MuJoCo trajectories in terms of distributional complexity, and explicitly qualifies the adapted RPC comparison as qualitative. It removes v2's HalfCheetah reward-gain/overfitting explanation while retaining the main limitations concerning model learning and application-dependent benefits.

D1.justification: v4 adds information about a single CPU running Ubuntu 20.04, SAC hyperparameter sources and the RPC implementation controls. However, v2's direct project-repository hyperlink is removed, and readers are now directed to supplementary material for complete hyperparameters.

E1.justification: v4 adds Hopper in the PASAC/RPC experiment (Table 2). Walker2d, renamed Walker, Ant, HalfCheetah, both driving scenarios and both custom Minigrid tasks remain.

E2.justification: v4 retains the PPO and DQN comparisons and adds RPC with 2-bit and 5-bit compression as a comparator for PASAC on Ant, HalfCheetah and Hopper (Table 2). RPC was discussed but not experimentally evaluated in v2, making this a substantive expansion of comparisons.

These disclosures do not establish increased repetitions for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Driving Table 1 is numerically unchanged, and v2 Table 2 is retained exactly as v4 Table 3. v4 adds deterministic-policy results in Table 4 and PASAC/RPC results in Table 2, including an Ant return of 6173.43 ± 442.87 for PASAC at k=1. M1.justification: v4 adds PASAC, with an entropy Q-critic and modified SAC actor loss, and a single-critic average-reward variant (Sections 5.2 and 7; Appendix B.1). Algorithm 1 also corrects the printed reward-gradient direction. The original PPO implementation is retained under the name PAPPO.

P1.justification: Technical proofs move from Appendix B into Sections 4–5, notation is incorporated into Background, method subsections are consolidated, and experiments are reorganized to present MuJoCo before driving. P2.justification: v4 adopts a single-column layout, replaces MuJoCo PCA plots with physical-coordinate panels, and adds comparative bar charts, trajectory grids and two result tables. The original MuJoCo table and driving illustration move to the appendix; driving PCA plots disappear, while retained training curves are repacked.

R1.justification: v4 adds Haarnoja et al. (2018), Kearns and Singh (2002), and Tiapkin et al. (2023), supporting the SAC implementation, a simulation-lemma connection and entropy-exploration context. T1.justification: Theorem 2 and its proof change from minimizing J+kJs to maximizing J−kJs, correcting their inconsistency with the original problem statement. Section 7 adds a derivation using the modified reward R+k log P for the average-reward case. The remaining principal results and proofs are largely retained or relocated.

improvement.justification: v4 corrects the central update's reward-gradient sign inconsistency and addresses important gaps in empirical validation through RPC comparisons, deterministic/stochastic controls and independent-run reporting. These substantially improve methodological coherence and assessability. The adapted RPC comparison remains limited, and losing the direct repository link weakens access information, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PARL research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renaming, relocation and reformatting.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix B retain original experiments and add PASAC/RPC comparisons and deterministic-policy evaluations.

C2.justification: V2 distinguishes bounded critics from successful imitation, using LSIQ as a counterexample, and interprets baseline reward/value instability. Section 4.2 newly acknowledges that IQ-Learn's convergence guarantee does not cover the practical chi-squared regularizer and that alternating SAC convergence remains unproved, materially qualifying the stability discussion.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five seeds and report means with half a standard deviation, including the hyperparameter analyses. V2 retains this uncertainty-reporting practice and introduces no new statistical test or estimation procedure.

E6.justification: New results in v2 Figures 3–5 show baseline reward/value dynamics and the point-estimate critic's failure to reach expert-level Humanoid performance. M1.justification: RIZE retains the distributional critic, adaptive-target regularizer, SAC updates, and value/v0 loss variants. P1.justification: The introduction and methodology are substantially rewritten and resequenced, including moving expectation and target-update equations into earlier subsections. P2.justification: V2 redraws and compresses plots, revises legends and colors, moves v1's combined demonstration-count performance plot into the main text, and adds reward/value grids and the critic ablation. R1.justification: V2 broadens the introduction with sparse-reward, preference-learning, and intrinsic-motivation literature, adds Muller et al. improvement.justification: V2 addresses two important weaknesses: Proposition 4.1 analyzes the full reward objective, correcting v1's regularizer-only argument, and Figure 5 directly tests the distributional critic's contribution. E6.justification: v2 adds crowd-reference results placing Black trisections lowest in responsiveness and toxicity results across religious leaning, sexuality, and age. Training budgets, evaluation cadence, evaluation episodes, and Table 1 hyperparameters are retained.

For example, the batch-size analysis now identifies a small significant benefit at 2000 samples. Moving the existing reparameterization and reconstraining studies to Appendix D is not a new ablation.

E5.justification: V3 generally reports five-seed medians and extrema. V4 uses 20 seeds for Sections 6.3–6.5, adds two-sided 95% bootstrap intervals using 10,000 resamples, and tests mean differences against High-Fidelity Only. Appendix boxplots add distribution summaries; the variance study and 24 additional settings retain five-seed reporting.

Figure 3 supports significant MFPG gains in all eight mild-to-moderate Hopper-gravity and Walker2d-friction settings, while Figure 7 revises v3's no-further-benefit finding at batch size 2000. M1.justification: The MFPG–REINFORCE procedure retains its control variate, shared-noise trajectory sampling, moving-average coefficient estimation, shared value baseline, and negative-correlation safeguard. P1.justification: Sections 3–4 substantially expand the estimator and sampling explanations, and Section 6 extensively rewrites the experimental narrative around statistical comparisons. Appendix E adds complementary difference plots and boxplots, splits the former combined benchmark displays, and retains the high-fidelity reference comparisons. Explicitly limiting the remaining five-seed evidence and expanding applicability limitations improve the calibration of its conclusions. C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's twofold contribution statement, and conclusion retain the same central claims: an upper-bound objective enabling recursive optimization, online neural cost-function learning, and favorable convergence against leading IRL methods. The expanded experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning UB's usefulness and the advantages of recursive optimization over naive online adaptation. Section 6.1 introduces expert-proximity when discussing Walker2d and describes highest average rewards in most environments, whereas v1 emphasized uniform superiority across its tested tasks.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds grid-search procedures, Adam and MPPI hyperparameters, covariance initialization, network details, runtimes, baseline implementation sources, and a statement that code accompanies the supplementary material. These substantially expand v1's sparse implementation reporting. However, Appendix A.2's general H200 hardware statement conflicts with Section 6.2's retained radar CPU description.

E1.justification: v3 retains CartPole, continuous MountainCar, and cognitive radar, and adds HalfCheetah-v4, Hopper, and Walker2d evaluations. These additional MuJoCo control tasks substantially broaden the empirical coverage.

E2.justification: The reported GAN-GCL comparator, attributed to Finn et al. (2016a), is replaced by AIRL, attributed to Fu et al. (2017), in the retained comparisons. v3 also adds SQIL and Adam-optimized UB to Table 1, and online-adapted GAIL, GCL, and AIRL comparisons in Appendix A.5.

E3.justification: v3 reports continuous-control networks with 16 rather than 32 units per hidden layer, MountainCar trajectories of 200 rather than 150 steps, and longer training horizons. It also introduces expert-normalized Walker2d reporting and per-observation update protocols for the online-adapted baselines.

E4.justification: The new UB-with-Adam comparison tests the empirical usefulness of the surrogate loss alongside conventional optimization. Appendix A.5 separately tests whether adapting competing methods to update after each observation closes the performance gap. v1 contains neither corresponding control analysis.

E5.justification: Continuous-control experiments increase from five to twelve Monte Carlo runs. v3 adds numerical uncertainty values to Table 1 and explicitly identifies learning-curve dispersion as standard deviations. This extends existing repeated-run reporting; radar retains five runs and a mean-only Table 2.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 replace the original scores: for example, RDIRL's MountainCar mean changes from 5110.09 to 4862.09, and its radar mean from 498.25 to 924.78. Revised settings prevent interpreting these as controlled performance changes. Extensive new results include Hopper, where SQIL's mean reward of 257.15 exceeds RDIRL's 220.79.

M1.justification: The upper-bound objective, regularizer, parameter and covariance recursions, and per-observation policy updates remain unchanged in Algorithm 1. Appendix A.3 expands the algorithm explanation without specifying a new RDIRL component.

P1.justification: v3 moves the lengthy Section 5 derivation into Appendix A.4, adds an explanatory algorithm walkthrough, revises experimental framing, and updates author information and front matter. These are localized organizational and explanatory changes; the abstract, introduction, related work, background, and conclusion largely retain their wording.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document from two-column to predominantly single-column layout, expands Figure 1 from two to four panels, and enlarges Table 1's comparator and task structure. It adds Walker2d and online-adaptation figures plus hyperparameter and online-comparison tables. The radar figure is redrawn and gains an expert reference curve.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for SQIL, MuJoCo, the imitation implementation repository, and two Ghanem et al. works supporting the optimization discussion. The related-work section and positioning around combining online learning with neural cost representations remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 adds a brief proof of Theorem 5.1 invoking Lemma B.3 of Humpherys et al. The upper-bound mathematics and recursive-update theorem are otherwise retained. The detailed Newton derivation moves from Section 5 to Appendix A.4, with corresponding equation renumbering.

improvement.justification: The UB-with-Adam and online-adapted baseline experiments address an important weakness in v1: limited evidence distinguishing the benefits of the loss and recursive update procedure. Additional MuJoCo validation and substantial implementation disclosures strengthen the empirical foundation and reproducibility. v3's blanket superiority wording conflicts with the Hopper ranking, and hardware reporting is inconsistent, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RDIRL research and provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures. All pages were inspected, including v3's Appendix A. v1 ends with references and has no appendix.

after.justification: Section 6 reports original results on the retained tasks and additional MuJoCo environments. Appendix A.5 adds experiments with online-adapted comparison methods.

before.justification: Section 6 reports original CartPole, MountainCar, and cognitive-radar simulation results, including learning curves and numerical comparisons.

C1.justification: The headline empirical claim expands from superiority on GSM8K to superiority across reasoning benchmarks and hardware configurations, including gradient accumulation. The conclusion newly presents robustness across down-sampling ratios and superiority over random and reward-only selection as contributions. The abstract and introduction also focus the framing on reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving inference saturation and diminishing returns when increasing rollout counts, and qualifies robustness when update subsets become very small. Its new limitations discuss mathematical-task coverage, prompt diversity as an alternative efficiency strategy, and selective sampling's incompatibility with strict on-policy guarantees. v1 lacks these substantive qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies Unsloth, TRL, AdamW, DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, the open-r1 integration and reward-function source, and an experiment-code URL. It documents L40S and eight-H100 implementations and explains batching across prompts. However, v1's constant learning-rate schedule and 0.01 warmup ratio are omitted; this is lost disclosure, not evidence of changed settings.

E1.justification: v1 trains and evaluates only on GSM8K. v2 retains GSM8K and adds actual MATH training and evaluation, substantially broadening the benchmark coverage beyond the original single dataset. Hardware and fine-tuning changes are separate experimental-setting changes.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates max-variance PODS against standard GRPO and only describes random and max-reward selection. v2 newly evaluates both selection alternatives against max-variance selection in Section 4.3 and Figure 4, substantially expanding the direct comparisons supporting the selection criterion. GRPO remains the principal baseline.

E3.justification: The main GSM8K LoRA comparison changes PODS from (n,m)=(32,16) to (64,16), and evaluation changes from every 100 steps to every half-hour. v2 adds MATH settings, full-parameter training on eight H100s with sequence length 1536 and gradient-accumulation controls, parameter sweeps, and per-step runtime and completion-length measurements. The earlier (32,16) configuration also appears in the new sweep.

E4.justification: v1 contains no empirical ablations. v2 tests sensitivity to generated rollout count and update subset size in Section 4.2, compares selection rules in Section 4.3, and examines completion-length behavior across these experiments in Appendix A. These additions directly investigate configuration sensitivity and the value of reward-variance selection.

E5.justification: v1 specifies eight training runs with different seeds and five test evaluations per checkpoint. v2 omits these counts while retaining bands described as 1.96 times the standard error. This reduces statistical reporting detail; it does not establish that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: v1's A6000 accuracy comparison is replaced by results under revised L40S settings and supplemented with MATH and eight-H100 results. Figure 2 adds runtime findings: PODS takes longer per step on one GPU but less time per global step on eight GPUs. Figure 4 reports max-variance above random and max-reward selection, and Appendix A adds completion-length results. These are not same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 changes its initial candidate from indices {1,...,m} to the first m reward-sorted indices, a limited procedural correction. The PODS objective, subset-based advantages, and max-variance selection criterion remain unchanged. The binary-reward theorem characterizes the existing criterion rather than introducing a different method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, and explanatory method passages undergo extensive rewriting. The brief experimental section becomes three organized subsections, and the conclusion becomes a structured discussion with limitations, future work, and broader impact. These are substantial narrative revisions beyond merely inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 adds a training-pipeline schematic as Figure 1 and replaces the original single accuracy display with paired accuracy/runtime panels across Figures 2–4. Appendix A adds completion-length Figures 5–7. The visual organization, captions, legends, and panel layouts are substantially expanded; neither version contains result tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for MATH, Robust Autonomy Emerges from Self-Play, Unsloth, TRL, ZeRO, and open-r1, while dropping the Qwen2.5 and LoRA references despite retaining their use. The positioning relative to DAPO, VAPO, and prior data-selection work remains substantially the same.

T1.justification: The central extreme-reward subset lemma and its proof are retained. v2 adds an explicit correctness and prefix-sum complexity proof for Theorem 1, formalizing the O(n log n) implementation already mentioned as possible in v1. New Theorem 2 proves the equal top/bottom selection characterization for binary rewards and even m, a bounded extension of the existing theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited empirical support: the added benchmark and distributed experiments test broader applicability, while selection-rule comparisons and parameter sweeps directly examine why and when PODS helps. Appendix A, additional proofs, implementation disclosures, and specific applicability limitations strengthen the paper further. Omitting run counts and scheduler details weakens reproducibility, but the more diagnostic evidence and better-qualified conclusions provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PODS research. Text, equations, algorithms, references, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 has no appendix; v2's Appendix A and its completion-length figures were included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original GSM8K and MATH experiments, distributed training comparisons, selection-rule and rollout-size ablations, and completion-length measurements in Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original GSM8K experiments comparing GRPO and GRPO-PODS with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, including accuracy curves and uncertainty bands in Figure 1.
