C1.justification: v4's introduction adds substantive claims of generalization from short, segmented solutions to long, unsegmented reasoning and superiority to self-consistency under matched compute, especially at larger budgets. These expand the original claims about data-efficient verification and test-time scaling.

C2.justification: v4 explains long-trace verification through implicit step extraction and interprets automatic-label results as showing independence from the labeling strategy. It removes v3's speculative suggestion to allocate verification compute by problem difficulty. Overconfidence, step-label interference, and computational-overhead limitations remain.

D1.justification: v4 reports code, data, and models as released rather than promised, discloses approximately 20% format/label acceptance and roughly 5K sampled chains, and clarifies binary ProcessBench scoring and GPU memory. However, v3's explicit rule for choosing the final beam-search answer by majority is omitted.

E1.justification: v4 adds evaluation of long reasoning traces without explicit step delimiters and an alternative Math-Shepherd training source (Sections 5.2 and 5.4). These extend the existing mathematical setting; the mathematics, science-QA, and code-generation domains remain.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain DiscPRM, LLM-as-a-Judge, majority voting, RLHFFlow-8B-Deepseek, MathShepherd-7B, and Qwen2.5-7B-Math-PRM. The added analyses reuse existing comparison methods.

It also adds Qwen3-1.7B-thinking evaluation on all 500 MATH-500 problems (Figure 11), beyond the retained 100-problem experiments. These are added evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: New Sections 5.2–5.4 investigate long-trace generalization, whether verification improves on spending compute on additional generator samples, and training with automatic rather than manual labels. Figure 29 adds a long-trace verification case. Earlier filtering, data-scaling, and difficulty analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The parenthesized percentages in the ProcessBench tables remain invalid-output rates rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Figure 11 adds long-trace and compute-matched findings. New Table 3 reports Math-Shepherd-trained ThinkPRM-1.5B F1 scores of 75.8/76.5 on OlympiadBench/OmniMath, alongside the retained PRM800K-trained scores of 76.3/75.7. These are results under alternative training conditions, not same-setting improvements over v3. Existing benchmark plots and Table 2 retain their results.

M1.justification: The synthetic-chain filtering, supervised finetuning, score extraction, and parallel/sequential verification procedures remain unchanged. v4 tests automatic labels and longer inputs without introducing a new algorithmic component; automatic labels were already contemplated in v3.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, method explanation, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting and condensation. Contribution bullets become a findings paragraph, the analysis subsections are reorganized, and Appendix G collects ThinkPRM examples. This exceeds localized language editing.

P2.justification: v4 adds the three-panel Figure 11 and automatic-label Table 3, moves the difficulty plot into the appendix, and expands the earlier verification example in Appendix G alongside a new case. Figure 4 adopts matching frequency axes, and the beam-search plot enlarges axis labels without changing results.

R1.justification: v4 adds Singhi et al. (2025) and the Qwen3 technical report, removes Li et al. (2025) on learning from demonstrations, and more explicitly positions ThinkPRM against GenRM's short, outcome-level verification. The broader related-work coverage remains.

T1.justification: There are no added formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations. Appendix E.1 retains the same verification-score calculation; additional mathematical passages belong to verification examples.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens practical validation: Figure 11 addresses v3's missing compute-matched comparison against self-consistency and tests long, unsegmented reasoning, while Table 3 tests reliance on manual labels. These address important evidential gaps. FLOP accounting remains underdescribed, and Appendix E.5's universal 100-problem statement conflicts with the new full-set test, but these reporting weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Process Reward Models That Think. Their text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and expanded material.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds long-reasoning evaluation, compute-matched analyses, and results from training with automatic step labels.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add claims of an unprecedented 96% experimental hit rate and potent activity against MDR pathogens. v1's claims concern computational performance, diversity, and filtering. v2 refocuses the contributions on biological embeddings, controllability, and experimentally validated discovery, dropping the separate Rank-filtering contribution.

C2.justification: v2 connects classifier feature importance to charge-mediated membrane interactions and interprets laboratory backtests as supporting specificity. It qualifies external comparisons through differing activity definitions and adds limitations concerning evaluated strains and novel peptide/property spaces. v1's specific template-conflict and ID/OOD failure interpretations disappear.

D1.justification: v2 documents CADS parameters, 276 classifier features and supporting libraries, classifier hyperparameters, early stopping, and laboratory selection/culture/MIC procedures. Reported generator training time changes from 24 to 72 hours, and classifier training time is newly specified. Laboratory peptide sequences are withheld and represented only by identifiers s1–s25.

E1.justification: v2 replaces the generator's AMPlify negative data with 774,405 Peptipedia peptides selected for predicted antibacterial properties. It adds signal/metabolic negative controls, evaluation on Tucker et al.'s experimentally screened sequences, and laboratory testing across 17 strains, including eight MDR strains. Template-constrained generation is no longer evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 adds AMPpredMFA, HydrAMP-AMP, HydrAMP-MIC, SenseXAMP-classifier, and PyAMPA to the classification comparison, and AMP-Diffusion to the generator comparison. New Figure 3 compares reported laboratory success rates with AMP-Diffusion, HydrAMP, CLaSS, and Joker; these are cross-study comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 expands the classification test mixture and adds AUPRC and LR+, replacing v1's HQ-only TPR/FPR evaluation. Generator evaluation switches from amPEPpy to HydrAMP-MIC, redefines diversity, and adds fitness and novelty metrics. Species-conditioned sampling increases from 2,000 to 10,000 peptides. New ablation and laboratory experiments introduce additional sampling and assay protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct generator embedding/scale ablations, single-versus-multiple-property tests, synthetic-negative distribution analyses, external-data robustness evaluation, classifier feature importance, and laboratory backtesting. Synthetic-data ablations are retained with expanded evaluation. v1's embedding-regression, explicit paired ID/OOD, template-matching, and filtering-stage analyses are absent.

E5.justification: Both versions average classifier results over five cross-validation folds. v2 additionally reports independent triplicate MIC assays in Appendix K.1. It does not introduce confidence intervals or a documented significance-testing procedure.

E6.justification: Classifier and generator results are extensively revised, with additional ablation and external-test results. General-classifier FPR changes from 5.82% to 0.3%, but the evaluation mixture changes, preventing a same-setting improvement interpretation. New Table 16 supports 24/25 peptides active against at least one tested strain at MIC ≤32 µg/mL; v1 has no laboratory results.

M1.justification: v1's two-channel hydrophobicity/padding representation becomes an embedding using five biochemical scales in v2 Section 3.1. Conditioning changes from full reference-derived vectors to masked-property training, optional attributes, and direct sampling from property ranges. The template-guidance procedure described in v1 is removed.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the introduction, related work, methods, experiments, and conclusion. Diffusion preliminaries and species-specific classification move into appendices; the main narrative emphasizes embeddings, conditioning, and laboratory validation. The appendix structure is substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: A single-column layout replaces v1's two-column format. Figure 1 is redrawn, conditioning results are reorganized into a combined figure, and the amino-acid frequency plot moves to the appendix. Several v1 analysis figures disappear, while laboratory curves, distribution plots, and numerous new or expanded tables are introduced.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially rewritten around representations, conditional control, and classifier feature families. New discussion includes AMP-Diffusion, ProT-Diff, protein language models, AMPpredMFA, SenseXAMP, and PyAMPA. Experimental comparisons and synthetic-negative justification also introduce substantial additional literature.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a masked conditional-loss formulation and replaces the formal diversity definition based on Levenshtein distance with normalized sequence alignment. Template-guidance derivations are removed. The DDPM/CADS mathematics, classifier weighting, and synthetic-negative N/L! argument are substantially retained or relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially closes v1's biological-validation gap through triplicate laboratory testing: Table 16 supports activity for 24/25 peptides against at least one of 17 strains. Direct embedding ablations and challenging external controls also strengthen empirical support. Withheld sequences, disagreements between MIC Tables 16–17, and unmatched cross-study comparisons weaken reproducibility and precise superiority claims, but the central laboratory validation represents a substantial overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmegAMP. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, allowing retained, revised, relocated, and removed content to be matched despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v2 reports original computational experiments and laboratory MIC measurements for 25 generated peptides against 17 bacterial strains, including resistant strains.

before.justification: v1 reports original classifier and generation experiments, conditioning tests, embedding-regression comparisons, and ID/OOD analyses in Section 5 and the appendices.

C1.justification: The framework and ensemble contributions remain, but v1’s prominent claim that black-box and white-box scorers generally outperform judges is removed. V3’s introduction and conclusion instead emphasize low-diversity failures, diminishing returns from additional samples, and dataset accuracy as a criterion for selecting judges.

C2.justification: V3 explains black-box failures through insufficient response diversity and recommends white-box scorers or judges in those circumstances. It adds judge-selection guidance based on dataset accuracy and a tentative token-wise explanation for BERTScore’s sampling behavior. These substantially extend v1’s applicability discussion.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies candidate temperature 1.0, default Optuna settings, hardware including a T4 GPU, and approximately 0.5–3 hours per model–dataset experiment. V1’s explicit uqlm v0.1.0 identification and Appendix A usage snippets are removed. These are documentation changes; the PDFs do not establish corresponding changes to previously unspecified settings.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate GSM8K, SVAMP, CSQA, AI2-ARC, PopQA and NQ-Open, retaining numerical, multiple-choice and open-ended question answering. Additional model configurations and candidate counts do not introduce different dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V1’s Gemini comparison includes a self-judge and GPT-3.5 judge. V3 evaluates GPT-3.5, GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Flash judges across comparisons, excluding Gemini-1.0-Pro judging. BLEURT also disappears from the evaluated black-box comparators. These changes materially revise the comparison set.

E3.justification: V3 adds GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Flash as generating models, including their white-box evaluations. Appendix C introduces evaluations at 1, 3, 5, 10 and 15 candidate responses. The main experiment retains 1,000 questions per benchmark, 15 candidates, five-fold cross-validation, and the AUROC, F1 and filtered-accuracy metrics.

E4.justification: V3 Appendix C adds a systematic candidate-count sensitivity analysis across 24 model–dataset combinations and an exact-match-rate diagnostic investigating black-box failures. These establish diminishing sampling returns and identify failures associated with nearly identical responses. V1’s appendix contains additional benchmark plots, without these analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-fold cross-validation averages without confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests or seed information. V3’s candidate-count sweep does not introduce repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Results expand to four generators and include revised rankings and new sensitivity measurements. For example, v1 Table 1 reports best-judge F1 of 0.75 for Gemini CSQA, while v3 Table 2 reports GPT-4o judge F1 of 0.89 as the best scorer there. The judge models and prompt differ, so this is a revised comparison rather than a demonstrated same-setting gain.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 replaces v1’s three-category judgments, mapped to 0, 0.5 and 1, with a 0–100 confidence prompt normalized to [0,1], including examples in Appendix A. BLEURT is removed from the suite. The remaining intended scorer procedures and weighted-ensemble optimization are retained.

P1.justification: V3 substantially compresses related work and method exposition, moves ensemble-tuning mathematics into Appendix B, places the revised judge prompt in Appendix A, and reorders the experimental narrative. The introduction, discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten, and the original code appendix is removed.

P2.justification: Separate Gemini and GPT-3.5 plots from v1’s main text and appendix are redesigned into four-model comparisons in v3 Figures 1–3. V3 adds an AUROC summary table, restructures the F1 summary by generating model, and introduces the sampling figure and exact-match table. Typography, headers and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: V3 narrows related-work coverage, removing the Fallah et al. ensemble discussion and several judge and similarity-metric references. It adds Jiang et al.’s long-form graph-based uncertainty work and Akiba et al.’s Optuna reference. Judge prompting is now attributed to Xiong et al.; the central positioning relative to BSDetector and PoLL remains.

T1.justification: V1 Equation 15 incorrectly uses the token-probability exponent L_i; v3 Equation 10 corrects it to 1/L_i, matching the geometric mean described in both versions. Other principal equation changes are equivalent condensation or relocation, including retained ensemble optimization in Appendix B.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the paper’s practical conclusions: stronger judge comparisons replace v1’s broad dismissal of judge performance, while Appendix C tests sampling budgets and exposes an important low-diversity failure mode. The corrected token-probability formula and added computing details also improve reliability. Removing usage examples and the package-version identification reduces reproducibility information, but the better-supported conclusions and applicability guidance provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors’ uncertainty-scoring framework and ensemble. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V3 reports original experiments using four generating LLMs, plus candidate-count sensitivity experiments and response-diversity measurements in Appendix C.

before.justification: V1 reports original hallucination-detection experiments using two generating LLMs and six benchmarks, including results in Appendix B.

C1.justification: The central claim remains efficient, reliable, repeated inference for expensive simulators through uncertainty-aware surrogate training. The abstract is substantively unchanged. The new novelty paragraph makes the existing E-Post relationship explicit, while MICP adds supporting evidence for the retained contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of CO2 surrogate misspecification, MICP prior mismatch, weak parameter identifiability, and wider predictive intervals. It also explains the simplified error assumption, surrogate-complexity tradeoffs, and limitations of the low-dimensional evaluations, with additional discussion of future misspecification mitigation.

D1.justification: Section 4.4 and Appendix C add MICP-specific measurement locations, priors, PCE specifications, and network choices while retaining existing implementation details. v2 also promises public code and data upon acceptance; this is a prospective disclosure, not evidence of an actual release.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates LogSin and a virtual CO2 storage benchmark. v2 adds MICP inference from actual calcite measurements at eight locations involving four parameters. This substantially extends coverage to observational data with a mismatch between measurements and simulator predictions.

E2.justification: The corresponding LogSin and CO2 comparisons retain their comparator membership. MICP uses existing methods: low-budget ABI, SABI, Point, and E-Post; full-budget ABI is unavailable for this new case. The expanded related-work discussion does not introduce additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Existing experimental settings are retained. The added MICP protocol uses 25 simulator evaluations, 10,000 offline training draws, and posterior comparisons without parameter ground truth. It introduces Scott-bandwidth KDE, predictive checks, and an original-versus-expanded prior comparison, increasing the k_ub upper bound from 0.0005 to 0.005. Its runtime experiment uses synthetic datasets.

E4.justification: Section 4.4 and Appendix E add substantial diagnostic analyses: prior-predictive mismatch, original versus expanded priors, surrogate extrapolation, Sobol sensitivity, remaining-parameter identifiability, and posterior-predictive checks. These investigate failure conditions and uncertainty propagation beyond the retained LogSin and CO2 analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports posterior median deviations and 95% SBC confidence bands. v2 additionally reports 90% prior/posterior predictive intervals and distributions of Sobol indices for MICP. These extend uncertainty reporting; no increase in independent training repetitions or seed counts is stated.

E6.justification: The existing LogSin and CO2 result plots and runtime findings are unchanged. New MICP results show posterior concentration at the original prior boundary, dominant sensitivity to k_ub, wider predictive coverage with uncertainty-aware methods, and runtime amortization beginning at four inference runs. These are added results under new conditions, not same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The core surrogate sampling procedure, training loss, and Algorithm 1 are retained. For the new MICP application, v2 omits the summary network and uses a spline coupling flow with fixed-location measurements, a limited architecture adaptation documented in Appendix C.2.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, method exposition, and existing case-study sequence remain largely intact. v2 makes targeted language and explanatory revisions to the introduction, objectives, and outlook, and integrates the new MICP section and appendix without reorganizing the established document structure.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template, typography, author-block layout, and figure placement, and adds eight MICP figures. Figure 2 is relabeled and repositioned, and several captions are refined. Existing result graphics are retained, including v1 Figure 7 as v2 Figure 11.

R1.justification: Section 3 expands substantially beyond JANA, Bayesian neural networks, and E-Post to discuss multi-fidelity methods, sequential inference, GP surrogates, structure-aware SBI, and additional likelihood approaches. v2 also explicitly attributes its uncertainty-aware surrogate foundation to Reiser et al. and adds misspecification-related positioning.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, training objectives, and Appendix B equivalence proposition and proof are retained. Renaming the PCE index from D to J and explaining standard Sobol indices do not introduce new theory.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support used simulated observations. v2 adds actual MICP measurements and investigates prior mismatch, sensitivity, and predictive coverage, substantially strengthening the assessment of practical applicability. Broader research positioning and clearer limitations further improve the paper. MICP lacks parameter ground truth and relies on prior widening, so it does not establish improved parameter accuracy, but its explicit diagnostics provide substantial additional evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UA-SABI research. All 16 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable. Retained equations, experiments, and figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original MICP parameter-inference, predictive, sensitivity, and runtime analyses in Section 4.4 and Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original posterior recovery, calibration, and runtime experiments for the LogSin and CO2 storage models, including additional results in Appendix D.

It strengthens multi-task positioning through comparisons with dedicated methods and a claim that joint tensor-adapter MTL was previously unexplored.

C2.justification: The new four-task discussion qualifies task-core benefits: the extra core improves the larger model's average but slightly worsens the smaller model's average. V2 also acknowledges limited single-task differentiation and hypothesizes analogous MTL extensions for other tensor architectures. Existing initialization-sensitivity limitations move to Appendix F without substantive revision.

D1.justification: Appendix D substantially expands Llama and baseline initialization, hyperparameter grids, learning rates, budgets and RoBERTa adaptation details. Section 5 adds a reproducibility statement. Appendix E revises pseudocode, including parameter registration and a condensed forward pass, although the latter introduces an undefined self.M_2 reference. This does not establish a new MetaTT code release.

E1.justification: V2 adds Commonsense170k training and evaluation on ARC-c, ARC-e, BoolQ, HellaSwag, OBQA, PIQA, SIQA and WinoGrande (Table 1), substantially extending v1's GLUE coverage. Three-task and four-task GLUE settings, including QNLI, already existed in v1 and are retained.

E2.justification: V2 Table 2 adds evaluated LoRETTA_adp and LoRTA baselines to v1's LoRA/VeRA/LoTR comparison. Tables 3 and 5 add dedicated MTL-LoRA and MoE-LoRA comparisons. The new Llama comparison also includes a zero-shot reference. These are substantive additions to the evaluated comparator sets.

E3.justification: The new Llama experiments introduce 7B/13B models, two-epoch training and best-result selection, and lm-evaluation-harness evaluation. Added baseline experiments introduce their own rank grids, configurations and training budgets (Appendix D.5). The retained MetaTT GLUE protocol, frozen classifier heads and multi-task sampling caps remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 Table 5 adds a controlled MetaTT-4D versus MetaTT-(4+1)D comparison for four-task learning; v1's four-task analysis showed task-core gradients and training curves without that control. Initialization, projection-selection, gradient and MRPC/RTE rank-adaptation analyses are retained. Consolidating the DMRG plots does not add an experiment.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly reports the new Llama results as single-shot, without uncertainty estimates, and states that selected LoRA reruns use MetaTT's seeds. Existing GLUE two/three-trial reporting, DMRG ten/four-trial counts and standard-error conventions are retained. No general increase in repetitions is established.

E6.justification: V2 adds Llama scores, tensor/MTL baseline results and aggregate four-task comparisons. Between v1 Table 1 and v2 Table 2, RoBERTa-large LoRA RTE changes from 53(0) to 87.0(8) following reruns of failed imported results; MetaTT-4D rank-32 CoLA changes from 63.3(7) to 64.0(1). The LoTR rank-32 row is omitted. DMRG rank-4 means in v2 Table 4 reproduce v1's figure legends.

M1.justification: The shared 4D/5D TT adapters, optional task core, forward update and bidirectional truncated-SVD sweep are retained. Algorithm 1 moves into Section 2.4 without changing its steps. Different initialization settings for the new Llama experiments and revised implementation pseudocode do not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, replacing the contribution list with question-led motivation. The DMRG algorithm moves from experiments into methods; related work, implementation settings and limitations are reorganized into appendices. A reproducibility section is added. These changes substantially reshape the narrative independently of the new experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with an additional task-adapter panel. V1 Figures 2 and 6 become v2's four-panel Figure 2, with existing rank-4 summaries moved into Table 4. New benchmark and settings tables, expanded baseline tables, boxed table rules, changed typography and wider text areas substantially revise the presentation.

R1.justification: V2 more explicitly positions MetaTT as extending LoTR/FacT's 3D tensors and LoRTA's head factorization, emphasizing multi-task use and TT-specific optimization. It adds discussion of VB-LoRA, Uni-LoRA, MultiLoRA, MoE-LoRA and tensor expressivity, alongside the stronger joint-MTL novelty claim. This substantially revises research positioning beyond relocating related work.

T1.justification: V2 Section 2.3 adds the formal condition r > (D/H)(1 - 1/H) under which MetaTT-4D uses fewer parameters than MetaTT-5D, and gives the multi-task parameter count 2Dr + (L + M + T)r^2. Existing factorizations are retained; no substantial theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the credibility of the central comparisons by rerunning failed imported LoRA results, adding relevant tensor and multi-task baselines, and moderating v1's superiority claims. Llama evaluations and expanded experimental documentation broaden the supporting evidence. These gains outweigh limited new reproducibility problems, although single-shot Llama results and inconsistent MoE-LoRA ranks between Tables 3/5 and Appendix D.5.6 still limit confidence.

Together these substantially improve the paper's reliability and practical interpretability while retaining its core study.

Appendix K adds a targeted analysis of distance-correlation trajectories during training with noise, without noise and with explicit curvature regularization. Table 4 additionally examines computational robustness as latent dimensionality increases.

Figure S5 specifies five runs for RGD conditions but one prematurely stopped explicit-regularizer run. Existing five-initialization and three-run reporting remains; the new utility and generative-fidelity tables report point estimates without uncertainty.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of practical usefulness and computational feasibility, which v1 left largely untested. C2.justification: v1 describes Jacobian-free magnitude estimation as an efficiency/stability compromise involving theoretically inexact omission. v2 instead interprets the Jacobian as covariance-based preconditioning and attributes harmful guidance to training-induced symmetry/PSD violations. It also treats adaptation to flow models as future work, whereas v1 described its construction as future-compatible with such samplers. The latent-diffusion limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents task/dataset-specific guidance values, DDPG inpainting hyperparameters, implementation choices for all six baselines, and the GMM model’s architecture and training recipe. The original image datasets and super-resolution/deblurring coverage remain.

The retained CelebA-HQ nonlinear-deblurring comparison expands from DPS alone to DPS, DAPS, and ΠGDM equipped with the authors’ nonlinear extension (v2 Table 2).

E4.justification: v2 adds Jacobian symmetry/PSD diagnostics (Figure 2), replaces v1’s surrogate-pairing and fixed-scale ablation tables with five-candidate guidance comparisons across three tasks (Figure 3), and adds a JAPS/ΠGDM scale sweep (Figure 8). E5.justification: v1 reports point averages without dispersion estimates. v2 adds standard-deviation ellipsoids in Figure 1b and mean curves with standard deviations across 1,024 GMM samples in Figure 2. E6.justification: v2 adds extensive task and metric results and replaces the AdaPS variant rows with JAPS results under revised guidance; dedicated noiseless-SR table entries disappear. Existing baseline numbers also change: DDPG’s noisy ImageNet SR LPIPS changes from 0.354 to 0.302, with PSNR remaining 25.55. R1.justification: Research positioning shifts from adaptive guidance scaling to bridging direct/proximal approaches through Jacobian analysis, including a new first-analysis novelty claim. v2 adds higher-order-gradient, covariance, latent-diffusion, and flow-model references, including Meng et al. and Bishop. before.justification: v2 presents a literature survey and conceptual taxonomy. Its empirical findings are attributed to cited studies; no original experimental or data-analysis results are reported.

C2.justification: V3 qualifies the connection between approximation and distinguishability using a 2ε separation. Section 4 newly conjectures that mean aggregation could distinguish super-polynomially many graphs despite being approximable by sum aggregation, explaining the role of arbitrarily close outputs. Remark 3.7 also restricts extensions beyond ReLU by requiring common-denominator control.

D1.justification: Section 2 newly specifies reduced-fraction representations, separately encoding numerators and denominators with logarithmic-length integer encodings, and assumes computations use this representation. V1 only refers to rational bit length. This adds computational representation detail; neither version supplies implementation or execution information.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or tasks for training or evaluation. The extension from constant to Boolean graph features concerns theorem domains, not empirical coverage.

E2.justification: Color Refinement remains the analytical reference, and neither version evaluates empirical baselines. The added activation-function citation and mean-versus-sum conjecture do not introduce comparator experiments.

E3.justification: Neither version contains empirical evaluation protocols, metrics, splits, or training budgets. Revised graph constructions and representation assumptions belong to the theoretical analysis.

E4.justification: Neither version reports ablations, robustness tests, or empirical case studies. The added graph example illustrates the revised combinatorial proof.

E5.justification: Repeated runs, seeds, uncertainty estimates, and statistical tests are absent from both versions.

E6.justification: Neither version reports measured performance or empirical qualitative outcomes. Changes to analytical bounds and mathematical findings are covered under T1.

M1.justification: Both versions analyze the same message-passing architecture with rationally weighted ReLU MLPs and optional graph readout. The revised aggregation classes and assumptions change the theoretical analysis, without introducing a new model or computational procedure.

P1.justification: The four-section organization and Appendix A remain. V3 edits the abstract and introduction, adds an Encoding and Bit-Length subsection and explanatory passages, moves the CR construction proof into the main text, and moves the information-counting proof into the appendix. Much of the surrounding exposition is retained.

P2.justification: V3 replaces the dense two-column format with a document-wide single-column layout, changing typography, headings, equation arrangement, spacing, and reference presentation. It also adds Figure 1 illustrating the revised CR construction. Neither version contains tables.

R1.justification: V3 adds Khalife and Basu (2023) and discusses its activation-function results relative to computability assumptions. Hardy (1999) and Hanson (1972) are added to support denominator-growth arguments. Most references and the broader research positioning remain.

T1.justification: Definition 3.1 replaces the earlier output-size-only logarithmic/sublinear framework with logarithmic conditions controlling both output size and common denominators. Theorem 3.8 extends the domain to Boolean features but drops the sublinear/subexponential cases of v1 Theorem 3.7. New aggregation lemmas and revised MLP/information-complexity proofs substantially change the argument; Remark A.1 sketches an exponential bound for mean aggregation. The CR construction changes from 2n+1 to 2n+3 vertices, adds two leaves, replaces binomial(2n-1, n-1) with binomial(2n, n), and removes the diameter-two restriction.

improvement.justification: V1 includes mean aggregation in its polynomial-bound class without controlling rational denominators. V3 introduces denominator-aware conditions and proofs, explicitly excludes mean, revises the CR counting construction, and corrects the graph-growth claim. These changes substantially improve the central contribution's defensibility and scope transparency, despite losing the sublinear extension. Local proof errors remain, including Lemma A.2's inconsistent O(log n) conclusion after defining n as input bit length.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same theoretical study. Their complete main texts and Appendix A are readable, and corresponding definitions, theorems, proofs, and presentation elements can be matched.

after.justification: V3 remains entirely theoretical. Its added graph illustration and appendix derivations are mathematical constructions, not experiments or data analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports mathematical definitions, bounds, and proofs, including Appendix A, but no original empirical results.
